It never appears in the output — it is the knife. Every section must advance it; material that is true but off the line goes in the bin, however interesting. 6: 7: - **One new concept per section.** A reader holds about four things at once. A section that introduces the validation contract AND the theming strategy AND the fallback policy teaches none of them — split or cut. 8: - **One idea per paragraph, stated in its first sentence.** The rest of the paragraph earns that sentence. 9: - **End sentences on the new information.** Readers place emphasis where a sentence lands: "the build fails loudly" beats "loud failure is what the build produces." 10: - **The reader has not seen the diff.** Name a thing before leaning on it — a flag, acronym, or internal name used before its introduction costs the reader a re-read. 11: - **Before shipping, prune padding.** Remove optional sections that add no distinct explanation; trim required sections while preserving their explanatory beats. 12: 13: ## The arc 14: 15: Use 4–11 sections total. Four distinct sections are required in this order: the setting → the gap / motivation → what we built → the short version. The setting comes first; the short version comes last. Each must explain its beat, not just carry its label. 16: 17: Optional sections belong before the recap and earn their place only when supplied evidence adds a distinct, reader-relevant explanation to the through-line. Plain language. Imagine the reader is sharp but new to the area. Include the one or two most load-bearing code hunks here, each introduced and explained (see "The key code"). 24: 6. **The honest trade-offs** — what the PR does NOT do, and why. Each trade-off gets the choice AND the reason. Use `

` sub-headings inside this section. 25: 7. **Alternatives considered** — what was rejected and why. One short paragraph per alternative. If none are documented in the materials, omit this section entirely; don't fabricate. 26: 8. **What the diff looks like** — file-by-file tour, usually as a 2-column table. Each row: file name (with status: "new" / "modified") + one narrative sentence. 27: 9. **A note on the test strategy** — optional. Only if tests are unusually structured (real-fs integration tests, fuzz, golden files, etc.). Skip for vanilla unit-test PRs. 28: 10. **What's next** — documented follow-ups, known issues filed, and any supplied priority order. Tie back to "trade-offs" where relevant; omit when none are documented. 29: 11. **The short version** — one paragraph for skimmers, at the END. Use identifiers from the actual source when they help explain the program. Check the title, subtitle, sections, recap, and narration for leaked review material before handing off. 36: - **Natural attribution.** Translate evidence notes into prose: use "The author reports…" or "The diff shows…" where attribution matters. Avoid passive ("it was rejected") — it's a tell of AI-generated prose. 39: - **Concrete > abstract.** Show the file, the constraint comment, the failure mode. …

`. The CSS turns the first letter into a 3.2rem drop-cap. Don't use it anywhere else; the doc loses its visual anchor if there are multiple. 59: 60: ## Code blocks 61: 62: Multi-line code goes in the section's `code` array, not in `content`. 67:   "file": "signal_unix.go",
68:   "source": "//go:build unix\n\npackage signal"
69: }
70: ```

72: - `lang` is a Shiki language id (`ts`, `go`, `py`, `rust`, `bash`, `json`, …). An unknown id degrades to plain text with a build warning.
73: - `file` renders as a small caption above the block. Set it whenever the code comes from a specific file — it replaces the old `// file:` first-line comment convention.
74: - Inline code is unchanged: `process.platform`, `foo_linux.go` in prose. You must still escape `<`, `>`, `&` there — `content` is authored HTML the build does not touch.

77: ### The key code
78: 
79: Use up to 4 code blocks total, enough to explain the central mechanism of a code change. Prefer one self-contained, load-bearing block for a simple change. Split only when distinct explanations need separate blocks, never to fill a quota. Content-only PRs may omit code. Rules:
80: 
81: - Show the code as it exists AFTER the PR — never raw diff hunks with `+`/`-` markers.
82: - Trim each block to its essential lines; elide the rest with a `// …` comment. Max ~20 lines per block.
83: - Introduce the block in prose, show it, then explain what the reader should notice. Never drop a block without commentary.

85: ## Diagrams (mermaid)
86: 
87: Diagram source goes in the section's `diagrams` array, not in `content`. Reference it from prose with a `{{DIAGRAM:i}}` placeholder (0-indexed, matching array order). Write it as raw mermaid — no entity escaping; the build owns escaping.
88: 
89: ```json
90: {
91:   "diagrams": [
92:     "flowchart LR\n  A[fetch-pr.mjs] --> B[JSON dump]"
93:   ]
94: }
95: ```
96: 
97: Referenced in `content` as `
{{DIAGRAM:0}}
`.
98: 
99: When a diagram earns its place: only when it carries structure prose can't — flow, hierarchy, sequence, state. A two-node arrow is prose, not a diagram.
100: 
101: Budget: 1–3 diagrams per document. Keep each small — roughly 12 nodes or fewer; a diagram that needs a legend is two diagrams.
102: 
103: Prefer `flowchart` and `sequenceDiagram`.
104: 
105: Every diagram needs a narration description in the manifest — the listener can't see it.
106: 
107: Rendering note: diagrams are themed to the document's palette and follow the light/dark toggle. If the mermaid package isn't installed at build time, readers see the diagram source as text — so the source itself should be tidy and readable.
108: 
109: ## Tables (file tour)
110: 
111: The canonical "what the diff looks like" table:
112:

FileWhat it does
file.ts (new)One narrative sentence — what role this file plays, not a diff of its lines.

125: ```
126: 
127: Mark new files with `(new)`. Don't mark modified ones. Don't add a "lines changed" column — irrelevant to the narrative.
128: 
129: ## Callouts
130: 
131: ```html
132: 

133:   
Worth saying out loud: the body of the aside.

134: 

135: ```
136: 
137: Max 1–2 in the entire document. They're for asides the reader needs but that break the flow. Don't use as a status badge.
138: 
139: ## Blockquotes
140: 
141: `
` is styled with a left rule and italic body. Use it for direct quotes from a spec, an RFC, or another doc — never to highlight your own prose.
142: 
143: ## Length
144: 
145: Word-count ceilings, not goals. There is no minimum; finish when the supported story is clear:
146: - Small PR walkthrough: up to 900 words
147: - Typical: up to 1800 words
148: - Large / multi-feature: up to 2400 words
149: 
150: If you're pushing 2400, you have multiple stories — pick the strongest one and let the rest go.
151: 
152: ## Forbidden patterns
153: 
154: - Lists of acceptance criteria with checkboxes (✅) — looks like a generated test report
155: - "Pros and cons" headings — essay voice doesn't use those
156: - Tables with status emoji (🟢, ⚠️, ❌)
157: - "TL;DR" at the top — the recap goes at the bottom; the *first* section is the setup
158: - Quoting the PR body verbatim — paraphrase, integrate
159: - Inventing alternatives or trade-offs not in the materials — research-driven, not imagined
160: - "We hope you find this useful" / "thanks for reading" / any sign-off
161: - Throat-clearing — a section that opens by announcing what it will discuss instead of discussing it ("In this section we will look at…")
162: 
163: ## When in doubt
164: 
165: Ask: would a reader who is sharp but new to this area understand WHY we did this, after one read? If no, find the one paragraph that's the bottleneck and rewrite it. If yes, ask the inverse: what did you include that the through-line doesn't need? Cut that, then you're done.

### `client.ts`

The request function previously sent the payload before checking whether credentials had expired, causing the first request after expiry to fail. It now checks the expiry time and awaits any required refresh before sending the payload. The response still returns from the same send call; streaming requests remain on a separate path that the author identifies for follow-up.

|---|---|
| `client.ts` | The request function refreshes expired credentials before dispatch so the first request after expiry uses refreshed credentials. |

## Key diff excerpt

**`client.ts` — request dispatch order**

```diff
diff --git a/client.ts b/client.ts
--- a/client.ts
+++ b/client.ts
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 export async function request(client, payload) {
+  if (client.expiresAt <= Date.now()) await client.refresh();
   const response = await client.send(payload);
-  if (client.expiresAt <= Date.now()) await client.refresh();
   return response;
 }
```

The expiry check moves ahead of `client.send(payload)`. Its `await` ensures that, when credentials have expired, refresh completes before dispatch. This single hunk covers the full change.

154: - Lists of acceptance criteria with checkboxes (✅) — looks like a generated test report
155: - "Pros and cons" headings — essay voice doesn't use those
156: - Tables with status emoji (🟢, ⚠️, ❌)

146: - Small PR walkthrough: up to 900 words
147: - Typical: up to 1800 words
148: - Large / multi-feature: up to 2400 words

152: ## Forbidden patterns
153: 
154: - Lists of acceptance criteria with checkboxes (✅) — looks like a generated test report
155: - "Pros and cons" headings — essay voice doesn't use those
156: - Tables with status emoji (🟢, ⚠️, ❌)
157: - "TL;DR" at the top — the recap goes at the bottom; the *first* section is the setup
158: - Quoting the PR body verbatim — paraphrase, integrate
159: - Inventing alternatives or trade-offs not in the materials — research-driven, not imagined
160: - "We hope you find this useful" / "thanks for reading" / any sign-off
161: - Throat-clearing — a section that opens by announcing what it will discuss instead of discussing it ("In this section we will look at…")

164:
